sentences.text: The name Massospondylus translates to 'longer vertebra'.
This animal is classified as a mid-sized sauropodomorph dinosaur.
Its skull was small, measuring about half the length of the femur.
The vertebral column consisted of nine neck vertebrae, thirteen back vertebrae, three hip vertebrae, and at least forty tail vertebrae.
As of 2019, the 'Big Momma' specimen is the largest and most complete Massospondylus and likely the most complete basal sauropodomorph found in Africa.
This massive fossil is divided into seven blocks, with the heaviest weighing approximately 35 kg.
Fossils include clutches of eggs with embryos, representing some of the oldest amniote eggs and embryos known.
Excavations between 2005 and 2012 revealed ten egg clutches containing up to 34 eggs each at the Rooidraai nesting site.
Fossil tracks show both hindfoot and hand prints with outward-rotated hands, suggesting quadrupedal movement in juveniles.
The genus Massospondylus was described by Richard Owen in 1854.
The first fossils of Massospondylus were described by Richard Owen in 1854.
Massospondylus is now considered to have been bipedal, despite earlier depictions as quadrupedal.
Massospondylus likely had a herbivorous or omnivorous diet.
A 2004 study by Galton and Upchurch found that Massospondylus cranial features resemble those of herbivorous reptiles more than carnivorous ones.
In 2007, Bonnan and Senter argued that Massospondylus was restricted to bipedal gaits rather than being quadrupedal.
The ossification of the thumb in Massospondylus embryos before other limbs suggests it had important functions at early developmental stages.
In 1993, Chinsamy-Turan found that Massospondylus growth was cyclic, forming one growth ring per year based on femur analysis.
Reisz and colleagues in 2005 suggested embryos were near hatching based on their size relative to the egg and advanced bone development.
Massospondylus swallowed stones to aid digestion, a behavior confirmed by the presence of gastrolites in its stomach.
A 2007 study suggested Massospondylus may have used its short arms for defense, fighting, or feeding, despite them being too short to reach its mouth.
Studies indicate Massospondylus grew up to 35 kilograms per year and continued growing until at least 15 years old.
Massospondylus is often classified within the family Massospondylidae.
In 1888, Lydekker classified Massospondylus as a dinosaur within the family Anchisauridae and the group Theropoda.
Massospondylus lived during the Hettangian, Sinemurian, and Pliensbachian ages.
Most remains are found in the upper Elliot and Clarens Formations of South Africa and Lesotho, part of the Stormberg Group in the Karoo Supergroup.
Massospondylus lived in Africa during the Early Jurassic, between 200 and 183 million years ago, from the Hettangian to the Pliensbachian stages.
It is debated whether basal sauropodomorphs like Massospondylus may have been omnivorous.
In 2007, Wings and Sander argued that the gastroliths in Massospondylus were likely not used as an effective gastric mill.
A 2025 study noted the hatchling's humerus is incompletely preserved, making reliable posture estimation based on shaft circumference difficult.
